headline: Northern Ireland batteries SI is made: QR-code labelling becomes a UK criminal offence from 17 October, 143 days before the battery passport
executive_summary: This Monday-to-Monday week has a hard legal keep and a quieter construction-data keep, and no healthcare instrument. On 25 September the Secretary of State made the Batteries (Placing on the Market) (Northern Ireland) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/1053), the domestic machinery that lets the UK enforce EU Regulation 2023/1542 in Northern Ireland under the Windsor Framework. The instrument comes into force on 17 October. From that date it is a UK criminal offence for manufacturers, importers, distributors and fulfilment service providers placing batteries on the NI market to breach Article 13 labelling – including, from 18 February 2027, the QR code that must sit on every battery and, for EV, light-transport and industrial batteries above 2 kWh, that must open the battery passport. Article 46 (identification of economic operators) becomes an either-way offence at the same time. Article 77 itself, the passport duty, is not listed as a UK criminal offence in Schedule 2; it still applies in NI as EU law. Construction’s keep is industry, not statute: on 21 September trade press reported that the manufacturer-led Manufacturers’ Information Hub had completed its UKRI proof of concept for a standard API and data dictionary between manufacturers and project teams, with tagging and tracking flagged for demonstrators. Healthcare published no new Scan4Safety, UDI, MDOR or medicines-packaging text. The UK digital product records call for evidence closed at 23:59 on 21 September with no summary of responses. Exchange for Change still has not published the product-testing guidelines promised by September. The one-year DRS countdown starts on Thursday 1 October.
cross_sector_themes: The first DPP clock is now a UK criminal-enforcement clock in Northern Ireland, not only an EU one
A QR code on every battery from 18 February 2027 is the data-carrier duty; the battery passport (Article 77) is a narrower, category-limited record behind that code
Construction is still building interoperability layers in industry while MHCLG’s product-library Alpha has not appeared
Operational clocks for 1–6 October (DRS countdown, Scotland HFSS, toys safety CFE) did not move this week and are now days away

sector_overviews.headline: NI batteries SI makes QR-code labelling a UK offence from 17 October; DRS testing guidelines still missing at the September deadline
sector_overviews.summary: Retail’s keep is SI 2026/1053, made on 25 September. It does not invent a new GB battery regime and must not be read as a Great Britain DPP mandate. It does make the EU Batteries Regulation’s placing-on-the-market rules – including Article 13 labelling and the February 2027 QR code, and Article 46 economic-operator identification – criminally enforceable in Northern Ireland, with GB unimpeded-access for qualifying NI goods. That is the live file for any member who places batteries, battery packs or battery-containing products on the NI or EU market. Nothing new landed on DRS barcodes, PackUK fees, Windsor Framework ‘Not for EU’ marks, Sunrise 2027 POS or e-invoicing. Exchange for Change’s news page still shows nothing after 7 September; the product-testing guidelines promised ‘by September 2026 latest’ have not appeared, and the certified reverse-vending-machine list is still indicated for early October. The UK digital product records call for evidence closed on 21 September; GOV.UK records the closure but has not published a summary of responses. Drinks members should treat Thursday 1 October as the one-year DRS mark, not a new specification day.

sector_overviews.headline: Industry product-data hub completes proof of concept; still no MHCLG library Alpha or GSR text
sector_overviews.summary: MHCLG, the Building Safety Regulator and OPSS published no new construction-product identifier, golden-thread instrument or product-library specification this week. BSR’s 22 September updates to higher-risk-building building-control and completion-certificate guidance only add a mobile-communications-mast completion route; they do not change golden-thread product identification. The construction keep is the Manufacturers’ Information Hub: UKRI-backed proof-of-concept work, delivered at the end of August and reported on 21 September, tested a standard API and data dictionary so manufacturers keep control of their own systems while specifiers, contractors and asset owners retrieve current product information. Tagging and tracking – linking the specified product to the physical product on site – is listed as a demonstrator theme. The roadmap is a minimum viable product still in 2026, a working prototype with early adopters by spring 2027 subject to funding, and some platform functionality in 2028. That is not a GS1 mandate and is not the MHCLG construction-product library. Construction exporters of batteries, or of products incorporating them, still sit on the NI batteries SI and the 18 February 2027 passport. Official Journal citation of EN 18239 and EN 18246 has still not appeared.

sector_overviews.headline: No new Scan4Safety, UDI or medicines-packaging instrument; NHS Scotland’s spotlight produced no published materials
sector_overviews.summary: Healthcare has no keep this week. Last week’s PSC/GS1 UK Scan4Safety report (17 September) is not repeated. A GS1 UK commentary piece dated 21 September restates that report and is the same evidence base, not a new development. The NHS Scotland Event took place on 21 September; the Cabinet Secretary’s published speech covers board reform and waiting times and does not mention Scan for Safety, and no session materials, slides or outcome note have been published. MHRA news in the window is sentencing in a long-running false-CE-marking fraud case (24 September) and routine licensing and appointments – none of it a UDI, implant-card, MDOR or pack-DataMatrix change. Draft Medical Devices (Amendment) Regulations 2026 remain the December file, with GB UDI still indicated to enter into force in June 2027. Trusts and suppliers should keep working last week’s 66% adoption evidence and the NHS Supply Chain Scan4Safety IMS framework, not wait for a new instrument.

items.title: Batteries SI 2026/1053 made for NI: QR labelling now a UK criminal offence from 17 October
items.summary: On 25 September 2026 the Secretary of State made the Batteries (Placing on the Market) (Northern Ireland) Regulations 2026, SI 2026/1053. From 17 October it is a UK criminal offence in Northern Ireland to breach listed provisions of EU Regulation 2023/1542, including Article 13 labelling – the QR code that every battery must carry from 18 February 2027 – and Article 46 identification of economic operators. This is Windsor Framework enforcement machinery, not a Great Britain digital product passport.
items.what_changed:
The Batteries (Placing on the Market) (Northern Ireland) Regulations 2026 were made on 25 September 2026 after a draft-affirmative instrument (ISBN 978-0-348-28391-4) had been approved by both Houses. They come into force on the 22nd day after they were made, which is 17 October 2026, except regulation 20(4), which waits for Article 11 of Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 (removability and replaceability). The Explanatory Note states that the Windsor Framework applies the EU law listed in Annex 2, as amended or replaced, in respect of Northern Ireland; Regulation 2023/1542 replaced Directive 2006/66/EC, which is on that list, and has applied since 18 February 2024 via section 7A of the European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018. This SI is the domestic enforcement layer.

Part 2 requires the UK(NI) indication alongside CE marking where a UK notified body issued the certificate. Regulation 9 makes the Secretary of State the enforcement authority for both the SI and Regulation 2023/1542. Regulation 10 and Schedule 2 create three tiers of criminal offence. Directly relevant to identification and data carriers: Table 2 makes breach of Article 46 (identification of economic operators) an either-way offence; Table 3 makes manufacturer, importer, distributor and fulfilment-service-provider obligations an indictable-only offence insofar as they relate to Articles 13(1) to (7) and (9) – labelling and marking of batteries – and Article 5(2) (sustainability, safety, labelling and information). Penalties for those indictable offences run to 12 months’ imprisonment, a fine, or both. Article 77, the battery passport itself, is not listed in Schedule 2.

Article 13 of Regulation 2023/1542, which the SI now underwrites with UK criminal law, requires that from 18 February 2027 all batteries be marked with a QR code as described in Annex VI Part C. For LMT batteries, industrial batteries above 2 kWh and EV batteries, that QR code must provide access to the battery passport under Article 77. For other batteries it must provide access to the labelling information, the declaration of conformity, specified waste-management information and related reports. The QR code must be printed or engraved on the battery or, where that is not possible or warranted, affixed to the packaging and accompanying documents. Regulation 2023/1542 defines a unique identifier as a unique string of characters for the identification of batteries that also enables a web link to the battery passport.

Part 7 revokes the Batteries and Accumulators (Placing on the Market) Regulations 2008 in relation to Northern Ireland, with savings for capacity labelling until Article 13(1) applies and for appliance design until Article 11 applies, and inserts a deeming provision so that a battery which meets Regulation 2023/1542 and regulation 3 of this SI, and which is a qualifying Northern Ireland good, may be placed on the GB market as if it met the 2008 Regulations. A de minimis assessment was prepared; net cost is estimated below £10 million a year. The Defra Batteries Team (batteries@defra.gov.uk) holds the assessment.
items.why_it_matters_to_gs1:
This is not a GS1 mandate and must not be reported as one. Regulation 2023/1542 requires a unique identifier and a QR code; it does not name GTIN or GS1 Digital Link. The connection for GS1 UK is that those EU requirements are now backed by UK criminal offences in Northern Ireland from 17 October, 143 days before the QR code and, for in-scope categories, the passport become mandatory on 18 February 2027. GS1’s provisional DPP application standard already maps the unique product identifier to the GTIN, optionally with serial for item-level passports, encoded in a GS1 Digital Link URI in a QR code or DataMatrix. That is how a member can meet Article 13 with a symbol that also scans at UK retail POS under Sunrise 2027 and, for drinks batteries in devices rather than drinks containers, sits alongside rather than instead of DRS work.

Two traps matter. First, every battery needs the QR code from 18 February 2027; only EV, LMT and industrial batteries above 2 kWh need a full Article 77 passport. Members who treat ‘battery QR’ and ‘battery passport’ as the same duty will over-build for coin, portable and small industrial cells and under-build for traction packs. Second, Article 77 is not a Schedule 2 criminal offence. A member who is ‘SI-compliant’ on UK(NI) marking and Article 13 artwork can still be in breach of the directly applicable passport, registry and unique-identifier rules in NI and on the EU market. If GS1 UK does nothing, battery and battery-containing-product members will buy non-interoperable QR payloads that do not encode a GTIN, while GB-only SKUs drift onto a second identifier just as the closed DPR call for evidence is being read. If members do nothing, February 2027 arrives with packs that cannot open a passport, cannot be checked at NI/EU customs against the DPP registry, and cannot reuse the same 2D symbol at UK POS.

next_steps.action: Issue a member note distinguishing three layers: (1) SI 2026/1053 criminal enforcement in NI from 17 October, (2) Article 13 QR code on every battery from 18 February 2027, (3) Article 77 passport only for EV, LMT and industrial batteries above 2 kWh – and map GTIN plus GS1 Digital Link as how those identifier and data-carrier duties can be met, not as a legal mandate

If you place batteries or battery-containing products on the NI or EU market, inventory SKUs against Article 13 versus Article 77, assign GTINs (and serials where the passport is item-level), and pilot a GS1 Digital Link QR that opens the required record – do not wait for a GB DPP
Battery passport builders: obtain EN 18219/18220 (already cited) and watch for Official Journal citation of EN 18239/18246; register in the EU DPP registry test environment before Q1 2027

Use the made SI, together with the now-closed DPR call for evidence, to brief Defra, OPSS and DBT that a GB digital product record should accept the same GTIN and data carrier rather than invent a second battery identifier for Great Britain
Monitor Defra/OPSS enforcement guidance and any appointment of a person to act for the Secretary of State under regulation 9(2); the SI names the Secretary of State, not GS1, as the regulator

items.title: Manufacturers’ Information Hub completes UKRI proof of concept for construction product data
items.summary: On 21 September 2026 construction trade press reported that the manufacturer-led, not-for-profit Manufacturers’ Information Hub had completed its UKRI-backed proof of concept for a standard API and data dictionary between manufacturers’ own systems and the specifiers, contractors and asset owners who consume product information. Tagging and tracking is listed as a demonstrator theme. This is not a legal duty and not a GS1 scheme.
items.what_changed:
IN Site (21 September) and The Construction Index (same day) reported that the Manufacturers’ Information Hub (MIH) has completed the UK Research and Innovation-backed proof-of-concept phase of its construction product information platform. The three-month programme, announced at Digital Construction Week in June, was delivered by the end of August. It tested how manufacturer databases could connect through a standard application programming interface, how information could be validated against a common data structure, and how authorised users could retrieve that information downstream.

MIH is a not-for-profit, manufacturer-led initiative. The published model is that manufacturers retain control over data validity, accuracy and access; the hub is an interoperability layer rather than another product-comparison database. UKRI’s Melissa Zanocco is quoted as saying reliable, direct access to manufacturers’ product information is an essential step in a more digitally connected construction sector, particularly for demonstrating safety and sustainability criteria.

The roadmap in the 21 September coverage is: a minimum viable product still placed in 2026, intended for demonstrator projects with manufacturers and main contractors rather than as an industry-wide service; subject to funding, a small-scale working prototype with early adopters by spring 2027; in-depth testing through 2027; and some platform functionality in 2028, with a pan-European rather than UK-only ambition. IN Site records tagging and tracking as an area for demonstrator work – a potential link between the product specified in design information and the physical product delivered and installed on site. The Construction Index notes the hub is intended to support environmental and safety compliance and to pave the way for digital product passports. Funding for the prototype stage is not yet secured. This is not an MHCLG, OPSS or Building Safety Regulator publication, and it is not the government construction-product information library whose Q3 2026 digital discovery was recorded in the 10 September Grenfell progress report.
items.why_it_matters_to_gs1:
The relevance is structured product data and, if tagging and tracking proceeds, unique identification of the physical product – not a new statutory unique-identifier duty. Construction already faces the Building Safety Act golden thread, the still-unpublished GSR, CCPI/PAS 2000, a promised national product library, and an EU construction-product DPP under CPR 2024/3110 in Northern Ireland. A manufacturer-governed API that moves property-level data instead of PDFs is useful only if the product on the far end of that API is identified the same way it is identified for merchants, DPP and, later, any UK digital product record. GTIN (and GMN where a model-level key is needed), carried in a GS1 Digital Link URI on a QR code or DataMatrix, is how that join can be made. MIH has not said it will use GS1 keys.

If GS1 UK does nothing, the hub can standardise attributes while leaving identifiers as manufacturer part numbers, BSI Identify UPINs or project-specific codes, and MHCLG’s forthcoming Alpha can treat that stack as the default back-end. Members would then run a parallel numbering scheme on top of GTINs they already use for merchants and for EU DPP. If members do nothing, they will connect a PIM to the hub without assigning GTINs to variants, and site scanning – the tagging-and-tracking demonstrator – will not match the code already on the pack. The opportunity this week is to offer MIH, CPA and MHCLG a concrete identifier pattern before the MVP is specified, without claiming GS1 is required.
